newsitem.title: USA: Staples merger means high prices-lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Staples merger means high prices-lawyer.

text.p: The government opened its case Monday against the proposed $4 billion merger of Staples Inc. and Office Depot Inc. arguing in U.S. District Court here that a combined company could raise prices on everything from file folders to photocopy paper.

With the CEOs of both companies sitting across from each other at the defence table, their lead attorney opened his case by declaring there was "no doubt" the merged company would offer consumers lower prices.

The five-day hearing before Judge Thomas Hogan will give both sides the opportunity to call witnesses and present evidence before the judge rules in June whether to grant the Federal Trade Commission a preliminary injunction against the merger. If he does, then the next step would be a months-long trial before an FTC administrative law judge.
The five-member Federal Trade Commission has already voted twice to halt the merger, but must prove its case in court.
George Cary, chief litigator for the FTC, presented a series of internal documents in which Office Depot and Staples identified each other as their major competitors for consumable office supplies.

"In 20 years of practicing antitrust law, we have something here I have never seen before -- real evidence, rich evidence from the companies' own documents," Cary told the judge. "This requires no guesswork."
Office superstores first appeared in the mid-1980s and dramatically lowered prices for office supplies. But Cary argued that the situation had changed at Staples.

A July 19, 1996, memo to Staples CEO Tom Stemberg said that Staples had "dramatic rate increases over the last five years in part due to our policy on all non-PSI (price sensitive items) and invisible items."

FTC lawyer Cary said that meant they could raise profits and prices on "invisible" and "non-price sensitive" items, where customers fail to notice price increases. But Cary said the fly in the ointment was competition from Office Depot.
The internal Staples memo said "Office Depot (has) worked on much lower margins and today their aggressive market prices indicates that is probably still true."
Because of competition, Staples would have to achieve "pricing parity" with Office Depot, an internal memo said. Cary said that translates into lower prices.

The government offered a series of exhibits based on internal company documents that showed prices were lowest on average where Office Depot, Staples and the third office superstore chain, OfficeMax Inc., competed against each other in any combination.

But they were higher -- as much as 14 percent higher -- where Staples of Office Depot faced no competition from another office superstore. Those 14 percent differences persisted even if the office superstores were near a K-Mart, WalMart, or another large store that also sold some office supplies.

In his reply, the lead attorney for the two chains, Don Kempf, said a merger would lead to competition. He said the merger was "no threat to the prices of consumable office supplies, no threat to the prices of office supplies (in general) and no threat to any market under the sun."
He demonstrated the competition he said exists by playing a Staples television commercial, a radio commercial and other public media presentations.
Kempf also said the FTC had tried and failed to get some witnesses to agree with its case.

For example, Kempf cited a deposition by the CEO of OfficeMax, Michael Feuer. Kempf noted that Feuer was first interviewed by the FTC. But in a 19-page declaration, Feuer said that, if the two competitors merged, he did not think there would be higher prices.
